assessment.nobel_worthiness: A new way of measuring time: the magic-wavelength lattice removes Doppler and recoil shifts while keeping many atoms in the interrogation, giving fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. This is precision measurement as a discovery tool, with direct consequences for redefinition of the second, relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and dark-matter searches.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and led the first demonstrations; Jun Ye's group drove the strontium clocks to the extreme accuracy and coherence that made the technique a field-defining instrument. The two-name credit is clean and covers the idea and the decisive demonstrations. Ye's shared work with Hall on frequency combs (already recognized in 2005) is a minor attribution wrinkle, and other lattice-clock groups exist.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed independently by many groups worldwide across Sr, Yb and other species, with international clock comparisons and ongoing roadmap toward redefining the SI second. The interpretation is stable and recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would prefer to wait for the SI second redefinition to make the impact explicit.
Role of other early lattice-clock groups (e.g. Yb and Hg efforts) in the credit, not resolved from the supplied list.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical readout and coherent control of single NV-center spins gave a room-temperature solid-state qubit and a nanoscale sensor for magnetic field, electric field, temperature and strain. This opened quantum sensing into biology, materials and condensed-matter imaging; it is exactly the kind of new measurement capability that changes what can be observed.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko made the first single-NV optical detection and coherent manipulation; Lukin's group contributed nanoscale magnetometry, multi-qubit registers and many sensing demonstrations. The three names form a plausible prize, though other groups (Hanson, Awschalom, Yacoby, Walsworth) also contributed major steps.
assessment.maturity: Highly reproducible with broad adoption and commercial instruments, and a clear stream of downstream applications. Recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Credit split between the early single-spin detection and the later sensing and entanglement work.
Several other leading groups are not in the supplied credit and could be contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Matter-wave interferometry with atoms is a precision instrument for gravimetry, gravity gradiometry, measurement of fundamental constants and tests of the equivalence principle. It translates the coherence of atoms into measurement sensitivity and has produced field-deployable devices.
assessment.attribution: Bordé gave the theoretical and early spectroscopic grounding for Ramsey-Bordé interferometers, Pritchard demonstrated the first atom interferometers with gratings, and Kasevich made the light-pulse atom interferometer and precision applications. The list is reasonable, but the history is spread across many groups, and Chu's contribution was partly recognized in 1997.
assessment.maturity: Established and independently confirmed, with continuing growth in space and field instruments. Some of the most striking claims (gravitational-wave detection, large-scale tests of general relativity) are still developing.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 1997 and 2001 cooling and condensate prizes may lower the perceived novelty.
Allocation of credit among Chu, Kasevich, Pritchard, Bordé and others is contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made strong, controllable light-matter coupling possible on a chip and is the architecture behind most superconducting quantum processors and quantum-limited readout. A concrete experimental platform with huge downstream impact.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf wrote and demonstrated the original scheme; Wallraff and Schoelkopf made the key experiments. I would pick the theorist-experimenter trio, though Girvin's omission is an uncomfortable cut. Superconducting-circuit work has already been recognized by a recent physics prize, which complicates the case.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many groups, with broad deployment. Recognition is arguably already partly covered by recent circuit-quantum prize decisions.
uncertainties: Overlap in subject matter with prior recognition of macroscopic quantum effects in superconducting circuits.
A fair three-person selection from four credited names excludes Girvin.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Superfluid-to-Mott-insulator transition in an optical lattice and subsequent quantum-gas microscopy turned cold atoms into programmable many-body simulators with single-site resolution. Experimentally impressive with a measurable effect on how many-body physics is studied.
assessment.attribution: Bloch and Greiner carried the decisive experiments; Zoller (with Jaksch, Cirac and others) supplied the theoretical proposal. Cirac is a natural fourth name, so the cut to three is not clean, and Jaksch is missing from the supplied credit.
assessment.maturity: Mature, replicated across many groups; the simulation claim is increasingly credible with growing quantitative benchmarks, though a quantum advantage on a classically intractable problem is not yet widely accepted.
uncertainties: Whether credit for the proposal belongs with Jaksch, Zoller and Cirac and cannot be fit into three names.
Unclear how decisive the simulation results are compared with classical numerics.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade supplies strong controllable interactions between neutral atoms and underlies programmable tweezer arrays used for simulation and quantum computing. Rapid progress, with larger arrays and high-fidelity gates demonstrated.
assessment.attribution: Lukin (blockade proposal and large-scale arrays), Saffman (gate proposals) and Browaeys and Grangier (blockade experiments) are all plausible. The four-name credit does not fit a three-person prize cleanly, and the Lukin-group and Browaeys-group experiments are partly parallel.
assessment.maturity: Active and moving fast, with strong reproducibility, but fault-tolerant operation and the long-term landscape are still developing; recognition may be somewhat early.
uncertainties: Platform competition with trapped ions and superconducting circuits is unresolved.
The attribution among many contributing groups is not settled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Prediction of flat bands at the magic angle and the subsequent observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity opened the field of moire materials, a tunable platform for correlated physics. Large field-opening impact, and the experiments are clear and widely reproduced.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the theoretical prediction, and Jarillo-Herrero's group performed the decisive experiments. The triple is a clean fit, though Cao and Fatemi, who did much of the experimental work, and other theory contributors are not credited.
assessment.maturity: Well replicated, but the nature of the superconductivity and the correlated states is still debated, so the interpretation is not yet stable.
uncertainties: The mechanism of the superconducting phase is not settled.
Credit for early experimental work by students and postdocs is not reflected in the three names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution is a conceptually original use of quantum measurement for secure communication, with fielded systems and a distinct quantum-technology industry. The principle is clear and lasting, although the physics is more a protocol idea than a new phenomenon.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard (BB84) and Ekert (E91, entanglement-based) are the natural trio. Wiesner's early conjugate-coding idea and the experimental demonstrations by others are not in the credit; the allocation between theory and experiment is open.
assessment.maturity: Mature in principle, with commercial and satellite deployments. Practical security issues, side channels and limited reach remain, but they do not undermine the physics.
uncertainties: The prize may be seen as favoring theory over the experimental groups that demonstrated QKD.
Real-world impact has been smaller than expected so far.
